messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Aroha was 24, a single pharmacist in Auckland, the sort of young man colleagues had once described as easygoing and light with patients, until his older brother died after a drunken fight outside a family member’s funeral. Aroha had not seen the blow itself clearly; what stayed with him was the chaos afterward, the crushed flowers by the cemetery path, the heavy smell of alcohol on the man who staggered nearby, and the feeling that something basic and decent had been ruined in front of everyone. In the months that followed, he found he could not tell the story in a clean line even to himself. When he tried, it broke into fragments: the wake, the black clothes, the sound of someone shouting, his brother on the ground, his own hands trembling. At times he could recall these pieces only with a strange numbness, as if it had happened to somebody else; at other moments the memory hit with such sharp guilt that he felt he should have done more, should have stopped it, should have somehow known what was coming.

The trouble did not stay in the past. Aroha noticed that people misbehaving—patients snapping at staff, a customer pushing past the queue, someone drinking too much at a gathering—could bring the whole thing back without warning. The same happened around funerals, cemeteries, and other grief-related events, which now felt loaded with danger rather than mourning. Even the smell of alcohol could tighten his chest before he had a chance to think, because it carried him straight back to that evening and the version of the story he still could not assemble properly. In those moments his body reacted first: his shoulders locked, his heart raced, and he felt already in danger while his mind was still trying to catch up. He knew these reactions were false alarms, yet he could not stop them, and the constant readiness in his body made him feel as if he were bracing for another blow at any moment.

As the weeks became months, the way he made sense of what had happened grew harsher. Aroha had come to believe that his life had been destroyed by the trauma, that nothing in it felt meaningful anymore, and that the happy person he used to be was gone for good. Those thoughts did not just color his mood; they changed what he noticed. He became more watchful for signs of disrespect, intoxication, or tension in public places, scanning faces and voices for the next thing that might go wrong. A slight smell of alcohol from a customer near the pharmacy entrance, or a family member mentioning an upcoming funeral, could pull his attention into a narrow, anxious tunnel. Because he had already concluded that disaster had taken over his life, he read these cues as proof that more loss was always close by. The more he expected danger, the more clearly he seemed to find it, and the more his mind returned to the same broken fragments of memory, each time with the same guilt and the same sense that the story could never be made whole.

At work this has become hard to hide. In the pharmacy, when a client comes in smelling of liquor or behaving rudely, Aroha’s body stiffens before he can decide how to respond, and he often finds himself overchecking, holding himself rigid at the counter, or pulling back from casual conversation for the rest of the shift. He has started declining family events if there is any chance of a memorial or a cemetery visit, and he avoids places where he might smell alcohol and be forced into that flood of feeling. The avoidance has reduced the immediate jolts, but it has also made his world smaller and his days feel more empty, which only confirms his belief that nothing meaningful is left. By the time he came for help, he was exhausted by living as though danger were always about to break in, frightened that his body would betray him in front of clients or loved ones, and more than anything hoping to find a way to remember his brother without the guilt swallowing everything else.
